product.title: Khmer 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Khmer (Cambodian): the pronunciation is printed right above every word in Khmer script, with short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Khmer builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Also included: a table of the 33 Khmer letters and their two series, subscript "feet", vowel signs, a guide to aspirated sounds, a page of Sanskrit and Pali words with a familiar ring, a list of classifiers, a summary of A1 sentence markers, and a glossary. Written for English speakers — each unit targets one of the spots that actually trip learners up, from the word for "yes" that depends on whether a man or a woman is speaking to a number system built on five.

cover_design.label: KHMER
cover_design.ringkas: A self-study course in Khmer for complete beginners — from reading the script of Angkor in a few sittings to telling the story of a trip to Siem Reap.
cover_design.catatan: The pronunciation is printed above every word; a word-for-word translation sits under every line of dialogue.

blocks.text: Khmer is almost always rejected before it is tried, and what puts people off is not the grammar but **the shape of the letters**. People open the first page, see a row of stacked curls like ភាសាខ្មែរ, and close it again, saying "no way". Yet Khmer script is the **oldest script still in use** in Southeast Asia — the earliest Khmer inscription is dated 611 CE — and it is the ancestor of the Thai and Lao scripts. It does look crowded and stacked, but it has only thirty-three basic letters, and nearly all of its sounds are ones you can already make.

Now the most important news, and it is worth reading twice: **Khmer has no tones**. Thai has five, Vietnamese six, Burmese three, Mandarin four. Khmer has none. ស្រី is said in a flat voice, much like the English syllable "sray", and it means "woman" whether your voice rises, falls, or stays level. That removes the obstacle that defeats more beginners than any other in the region. If you ever gave up on Thai or Vietnamese because of the tones, Khmer is a door standing wide open.

The genuinely hard parts lie elsewhere, and this course will not pretend otherwise. First, **the letters come in two series**. ក and គ are both read *k*, but the vowel attached to them sounds different — កា is *kaa*, គា is *kiè*. One vowel sign has two sounds, and the letter in front of it decides which. Second, **letters can stack**: a second consonant drops below the first as a "foot" (ជើង), so ស្រ, ខ្ញ, ព្រ look like one shape but are two letters. Third, ⚠️ **the word for "yes" depends on whether the speaker is a man or a woman**: men say បាទ, women say ចាស. You use it in your very first sentence, so unit 1 covers it thoroughly.

The good news far outweighs the bad. **Khmer word order is the same as English**: subject – verb – object. ខ្ញុំញ៉ាំបាយ is "I eat rice", word for word. **Adjectives come after the noun**: ផ្ទះធំ = "house big", not "big house". **Possession needs no word at all**: ផ្ទះខ្ញុំ = "house I" = "my house". Khmer also **has no articles**, **no grammatical gender**, **no plural endings**, and **its verbs never change form** — ទៅ stays ទៅ whether the subject is I, you, she, yesterday, or tomorrow. There is not a single verb table to memorize. If French or Spanish verb endings ever wore you down, this is a holiday.

There is one more gift. **You already know a few Khmer words without ever having studied them.** Khmer took its learned vocabulary from **Sanskrit and Pali** — the same classical languages that gave English *guru*, *karma*, *dharma*, *pundit*, and *naga*. គ្រូ is a teacher, a guru. កម្ម is karma, ធម៌ is dharma, បណ្ឌិត is a scholar — a pundit. ភាសា (language), មនុស្ស (human being), សិស្ស (student), ភូមិ (village), ចិត្ត, គុណ, ទុក្ខ, សត្វ, រូប, នាម, ជាតិ, ពេល, ប្រទេស, ពិសេស — all of them came into Khmer from India centuries ago. A special page in this course collects them, and the units flag them so you can stop and enjoy them. The highlight comes in unit 10, where you discover that **Khmer names its weekdays after the same seven planets as English and French do**.

Three things are deliberately different from other Khmer books. First, **the pronunciation is printed right above each Khmer word**, not on a separate line, so your eyes don't jump back and forth and lose their place mid-sentence. This is not decoration: Khmer is written **without spaces between words** — spaces only separate phrases — and without the pronunciation above, beginners are sure to cut words in the wrong place. Second, every line of dialogue has a **word-for-word translation** showing the original order, even when it sounds odd, because that is exactly where the lesson lies. Third, each unit targets **one typical trap for English speakers**, and names it openly instead of hiding it in a footnote.

One last thing. Sixteen million people speak Khmer, and almost no foreigners bother to learn it — in Siem Reap, a city visited by millions of tourists every year, the foreign word heard most often is still "hello". As a result, the reward comes very fast. Say សួស្ដី with your palms pressed together to a vendor at Psar Chas and watch what happens to their face. In a country rarely visited by people willing to make the effort, ten words are enough to be treated as a guest, not a tourist.

This course is designed for self-study, without a teacher, twenty to thirty minutes per sitting. One unit = one sitting. Don't do two units at once, even if it feels easy — Khmer has a way of piling up, and a rushed unit will catch up with you in unit 12, where the verb markers start to stack.
Suggested order within a unit

items: **Read the title and the "By the end of this unit" list.** Those five lines are the unit's promise. If at the end you can do all five without looking, the unit is done.

**Read the dialogue aloud, twice.** Once looking at the pronunciation above the letters, and once more covering the pronunciation with your finger and trying to read the Khmer script directly. That second round is what teaches the script — not the letter table.

**Don't make your voice go up and down.** Khmer has no tones. Learners who have dabbled in Thai or Mandarin often bring along a habit of singing words; here that habit makes you harder to understand. Speak as evenly as a newsreader.
**Only then read the translation.** Reversing this order is the most common mistake: if you read the meaning first, your eyes will never really look at the Khmer sentence.
**Pay attention to the literal line.** The small line under each sentence shows the original Khmer order. That is where you learn to think in Khmer instead of translating from English.
**Do the exercises by hand, on paper.** Answering in your head feels faster and works far worse. The answer key is on the same page, so cover it with paper first.

blocks.text: If you have thirty extra minutes a week

Copy out each unit's dialogue by hand, letter by letter, without the pronunciation. Copying Khmer script forces your eyes to notice the subscript feet and vowel signs that slip past when you read quickly. Ten minutes of copying does more than an hour of staring at a letter table.

front.title: Khmer script: thirty-three letters and two series

blocks.text: Khmer script descends from the Pallava script of South India — the same ancestor as the Thai, Lao, Burmese, Javanese, and Balinese scripts. The basic logic is simple: **every consonant letter already carries a built-in vowel**, and a second consonant attached to it drops down as a "foot" below the first. Khmer calls this ជើង (*cheung*, "foot").
The first thing to accept: two series

This is the hardest part of the whole course, and it is better faced now. Khmer's thirty-three letters are divided into **two series**: the **អ** series (a-series, fifteen letters) and the **ឲ** series (o-series, eighteen letters). The series doesn't change the consonant sound — ក and គ are both read *k*. What it changes is **the sound of the vowel attached to it**.

So one vowel sign has two sounds, and the letter in front of it tells you which. That sounds heavy, and it is — but there are two real consolations. First, **you don't need to memorize it to use this course**: the pronunciation is printed above every word, so you absorb it through repetition, not through tables. Second, the series are not random — the o-series letters are almost all "voiced" letters in the original Indian alphabet (g, j, d, b, m, n, y, r, l, w).

blocks.title: Two signs that move a letter to the other series
items: **៉ (musikatoan)** pulls an o-series letter into the a-series. It lets sounds that have no letter of their own be written: ម + ៉ = ម៉ (*maa*), ន + ៉ = ន៉.
**៊ (triisap)** does the opposite: it pulls an a-series letter into the o-series. ស + ៊ = ស៊ (*sòò*), used among other things to write foreign names such as ស៊ីម (*siim*).
Both turn up mostly in loanwords and place names, so get to know their shape early, even though you don't need to memorize them.

blocks.text: Subscript feet (ជើង)

When two consonants meet with no vowel between them, the second is written **below** the first in a small form. ស + ្រ = ស្រ (*sr*), ខ + ្ញ = ខ្ញ (*khny*), ព + ្រ = ព្រ (*pr*). The foot usually looks like a shrunken version of the full letter, but a few change quite a lot — ្រ, ្ន, and ្ម are the three you will meet most often.

⚠️ Note that clusters such as *khny*, *pht*, and *thng* are **said truly together**, with no linking vowel. English speakers almost always slip an "uh" in between — *khuh-nyom* for ខ្ញុំ, *thuh-ngay* for ថ្ងៃ. That sounds like a foreigner spelling the word out. The fix is simple: start the first consonant, then release all the rest in one go.

The thirty-three basic letters, arranged by where the sound is made in the mouth — from the back of the tongue to the lips, an order inherited from India (k-group, ch-group, t-group, p-group). The "series" column tells you the built-in vowel. Letters marked ° appear almost only in Pali-Sanskrit loanwords, so just learn to recognize them; don't drill them.

blocks.text: Khmer numerals

Khmer numerals are still used everywhere — market prices, house numbers, bus numbers, dates in the newspaper. Their shapes are based on five: ០ to ៥ stand on their own, while ៦ to ៩ add a stroke to ៥. They are also read on a base of five, which unit 5 covers in full.

front.title: Khmer sounds: no tones, but a puff of air

blocks.text: This course uses a pronunciation guide built for English speakers. It is not a scientific system — it follows the spellings you see on Cambodian maps and signs (*Khmer*, *Phnom Penh*, *Kampong Cham*), plus a few marks for vowels English doesn't have. One page of rules, and after that you can read the whole course aloud and be understood.
Rule one: an h AFTER k, ch, t, p means a puff of air

Khmer distinguishes k from aspirated k, ch from aspirated ch, t from aspirated t, and p from aspirated p. The difference is just a small puff of breath after the consonant. This course writes the puff as an **h after the consonant**: *kh, chh, th, ph*. Without the h, there is **no** puff: *k* as in **skin**, *t* as in **stop**, *p* as in **spin**, and *ch* somewhere between the "j" in **jam** and the "ch" in **itchy**.

blocks.title: ⚠️ ph is not f, th is not "think"
items: *ph* is **never** an **f** as in "photo". ភ្នំពេញ is spelled *Phnom Penh* and pronounced *phnum-peñ* — a p with a puff, then n. ភ is not f at all.
*th* is **never** the English sound in *think* or *this*. ថ is simply t with a puff of air, as in **top**.
*kh* is not the rough sound in Scottish *loch* or German *Bach* — it is just k with a puff, as in **kin**. And *chh* is ch with a puff, as in **church**; plain *ch* has none.

So: **ខ = *kh*, ឆ = *chh*, ថ = *th*, ផ = *ph***. Hold a hand in front of your mouth: these should hit it; *k, ch, t, p* should not. If you forget the puff you will still be understood — but ថ្លៃ (*thlay*, expensive) and ត្លៃ will sound the same, and haggling will get harder.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **An h AFTER a vowel is a different sound** — a final breathy h, as in "ah!" or "oh!". ផ្ទះ (*phteah*, house) ends with an h you can actually hear. So the position of the h decides its job: after a consonant = a puff, after a vowel = a final sound.

blocks.text: **Long vowels are written double**: *aa, ii, uu, òò, éé*. Length really does change the meaning in Khmer, so don't ignore it — but the good news is that you don't have to memorize which vowels are long: the pronunciation is printed above every word. Plain vowels have their "continental" values, as in Spanish or Italian: *a* as in "father", *i* as in "machine", *u* as in "rule", *o* as in "go" (pure, no w-glide); *ay* rhymes with "eye", *ey* with "they", *ao* with "cow".
Rule three: don't sing

Once more, because this is the rule broken most often: **Khmer has no tones**. Speak with a flat, natural sentence melody. The only thing that rises and falls is the melody of the whole sentence — rising slightly at the end of a question, just as in English. Individual words have no pitch of their own.

front.title: Sanskrit and Pali words with a familiar ring

blocks.text: Khmer, like Thai and Indonesian, absorbed thousands of words from **Sanskrit and Pali** — through the kingdoms of Funan, Chenla, and Angkor, and through Buddhism. Some of these words also traveled to English, so you start with a handful already in your pocket: *guru*, *karma*, *dharma*, *pundit*, *naga*. The others are worth learning as a family: once you know the root, you will spot it again and again on temple signs, in names, and in the news.

blocks.text: Mind, religion, and values

blocks.title: ⚠️ Six words whose meaning has shifted — careful
items: **ភ័យ** (*phey*) = **FEAR**. Sanskrit *bhaya* meant both fear and danger; Khmer kept the feeling, not its cause. Danger in Khmer is គ្រោះថ្នាក់ (*kroah-thnak*).
**លោក** (*lok*) = **MR., SIR** — an everyday form of address, not the Sanskrit *loka*, "world". The world in Khmer is ពិភពលោក (*pi-phup-lok*).
**សុខ** (*sok*) = **HEALTHY, AT PEACE**, not "happy" like Sanskrit *sukha*. Happy is សប្បាយ (*sappaay*). The greeting សុខសប្បាយទេ? means "healthy and happy?".
**បុណ្យ** (*bon*) = **FESTIVAL, MERIT** — the merit you earn by good deeds, and the festival where you earn it. បុណ្យអុំទូក is the Water Festival with its boat races.
**ចិត្ត** (*chet*) = **HEART or MIND** as the seat of feelings. ចូលចិត្ត literally means "enter the heart" and means "to like".
**ប្រទេស** (*pra-teh*) = **COUNTRY**, not "region" like Sanskrit *pradeśa*. Cambodia is ប្រទេសកម្ពុជា.

blocks.text: And save one surprise for unit 10: all seven Khmer **weekday names** are Sanskrit names of the sun, the moon, and the five visible planets — the same scheme behind English *Sunday* and *Monday* and French *mardi* (Mars) and *mercredi* (Mercury). ចន្ទ is the Moon, អង្គារ is Mars, ពុធ is Mercury, សុក្រ is Venus. Not just similar: the same idea.

back.title: Classifiers: the list you'll actually use

blocks.text: Khmer counts things in the order **noun – number – classifier**: សៀវភៅ ពីរ ក្បាល = "book two head" = two books. English has a faint echo of this in "three *head* of cattle" or "two *sheets* of paper"; Khmer simply does it with almost every noun, and always puts the classifier after the number.

The second piece of good news: Khmer classifiers are **much more relaxed** than Thai or Burmese ones. In everyday conversation Cambodians often drop them altogether and just say សៀវភៅ ពីរ. So don't memorize a long list. The rows below cover nearly all A1 conversation.

blocks.title: Two ways out if you forget
items: **Repeat the noun as its own classifier.** ថ្ងៃ បី ថ្ងៃ ("day three day") is perfectly correct and very common. This escape route always works.
**Or just leave it out.** សៀវភៅ ពីរ sounds a little casual, but it is never wrong. Cambodians do it all day long.

blocks.text: Dates run **day – month – year**, as in British English: ថ្ងៃទី ១៧ ខែ មេសា ឆ្នាំ ១៩៧៥ = the 17th day of the month of April, year 1975. All the month names are borrowed: មករា, កុម្ភៈ, មីនា, មេសា, ឧសភា, មិថុនា, កក្កដា, សីហា, កញ្ញា, តុលា, វិច្ឆិកា, ធ្នូ — and all twelve are **Sanskrit zodiac signs**: Makara (Capricorn), Kumbha (Aquarius), Mina (Pisces), Mesha (Aries), Vrishabha (Taurus), Mithuna (Gemini), Karkata (Cancer), Simha (Leo), Kanya (Virgo), Tula (Libra), Vrischika (Scorpio), Dhanu (Sagittarius).

English gets by with one "you". Khmer chooses its pronoun according to **who you are talking to** — older or younger, a stranger, a monk, a child. Think of it as choosing between "sir", "ma'am", and a first name, every time you speak.

blocks.text: If you have reached this page after genuinely working through all twenty units, you are now at full A1: you can introduce yourself, haggle, order food you are able to eat, tell the time, ask for directions, talk about something that has already happened, and decline politely without saying the word "no". That is no small thing. Most foreigners who live in Cambodia for years never get this far.
Three things that will get you to A2 fastest

items: **Read signs.** Khmer script is on every shop, every bus, every packet of noodles. Reading signs for ten minutes a day teaches the script far faster than any letter table — and you already have what you need.

**Collect the Sanskrit words you come across.** Every time you recognize a root you have met before — or one that English borrowed too — write it down. The list will grow much faster than you expect, and every word on it is already half yours.

**Speak flat.** The biggest mistake learners make in their first year is not grammar but bringing the melody of Thai or Mandarin — or the heavy word stress of English — into Khmer sentences. Record yourself once a week and listen for whether you are singing.

blocks.text: What this course has not covered

Four things have been deliberately postponed because they don't belong to A1. **Layered respect language** — Khmer has separate vocabulary for speaking to monks and to the royal family (ឆាន់ for "eat" when a monk eats, សោយ for a king); you will hear it on television and at the wat, and for now it is enough to recognize it. **Complex sentences** with ដែល ("who, which") as the link. **Serial verbs** that string three or four verbs together in one sentence. And **Khmer handwriting**, whose shapes differ enough from print to deserve practice of their own.
Farewell

Cambodians have a habit that guidebooks rarely mention: they remember foreigners who try. Not the fluent ones — the ones who try. Your Khmer sentences may stumble, your word order may occasionally flip, your puffs of air may vanish; what they hear is that you made the effort. សូមអោយមានសុខភាពល្អ — may you always be healthy, and see you in Cambodia.
